\label{p:M}
Let $\mathcal{P} = \langle x_1, \dots, x_n| r_1, \dots, r_m \rangle$ be a 
  presentation of a group $G_{\mathcal{P}}$. Then there is an algorithmically
  constructible compact $5$-manifold $M_{\mathcal{P}}$ with
  boundary, possessing the following properties:
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $M_{\mathcal{P}}$ is smoothly embeddable in ${\mathbb{R}}^5$;
    \item $\pi_1(M_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong  \pi_1(\partial  M_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong G_{\mathcal{P}}$; and
    \item if $G_{\mathcal{P}}$ is trivial, then $H_2(\partial M)$ is a free product of $2k$
      copies of ${\mathbb{Z}}$ where $k$ is the deficiency of $\mathcal{P}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: The first step is to build a simplicial 2-complex K_P such that pi_1(M_P) cong G_P. This simplicial complex can be built by subdividing a CW-complex obtained from a wedge of n 1-spheres (each 1-sphere is oriented and corresponds to one of the generators) and attaching 2-cells to the 1-spheres according to the relations in P. The complex K_P linearly embeds in R^5 by a general position argument. Now we pick three sufficiently small numbers rho_0 > rho_1 > rho_2 > 0 and we consider a manifold M'_P subseteq R^5 consisting of all points in R^5 in a distance at most rho_i from some i-face of K_P. If the radii rho_i are suitably chosen, then M'_P deformation retracts to K_P. Thus pi_1(M'_P) cong pi_1(K_P) cong G_P. By `smoothening the corners' we obtain the desired smooth manifold M_P smoothly embedded in R^5 with pi_1(M_P) cong pi_1(M'_P) cong G_P (M_P is homotopy equivalent with M'_P). But it also follows that pi_1(M_P) cong pi_1(partial M_P); see the proof of Lemma~3 in. This establishes (i) and (ii). For (iii), if G_P is trivial, we first note that H_2(partial M) (and H^2(partial M)) are free Z-modules (there is no torsion). Indeed, this follows from the Poincaré duality and the universal coefficient theorem (using that H_1(partial M) = 0). Thus it is sufficient to perform computations over Q. Next we note that the Euler characteristic of K_P equals 1 - n + m = 1 + k. (Computing the Euler characteristic is easy. This formula is, for example, mentioned below proof of Theorem~2.7 in Chapter I. of.) The Euler characteristic can be equivalently expressed as beta_0(K_P) - beta_1(K_P) + beta_2(K_P). If G_P is trivial, then K_P is simply connected and thus beta_1(K_P) = 0. Because K_P is connected, we also get beta_0(K_P) = 1. Thus we deduce that beta_2(K_P) = k. Consequently, beta_2(M_P) = k as M_P and K_P are homotopy equivalent. Finally, by `half lives, half dies'; see or (in the latter case, the proof is given only in dimension 3 but it extends to odd dimensions), we get beta_2(partial M_P) = 2k.

The first step is to build a simplicial $2$-complex $K_{\mathcal{P}}$ such that
  $\pi_1(M_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong G_{\mathcal{P}}$. This simplicial complex can be built by
  subdividing
  a CW-complex obtained from a wedge of $n$ 1-spheres (each 1-sphere is
  oriented and corresponds to one of the generators) and attaching $2$-cells to
  the 1-spheres according to the relations in $\mathcal{P}$. 

  The complex $K_{\mathcal{P}}$ linearly embeds in ${\mathbb{R}}^5$ by a general position argument.
  Now we pick three sufficiently small numbers $\rho_0 > \rho_1 > \rho_2 > 0$
  and we consider a manifold $M'_{\mathcal{P}} \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^5$ consisting of all points in
  ${\mathbb{R}}^5$ in a distance at most $\rho_i$ from some $i$-face of $K_{\mathcal{P}}$. If the
  radii $\rho_i$ are suitably chosen, then $M'_{\mathcal{P}}$ deformation retracts to
  $K_{\mathcal{P}}$. Thus $\pi_1(M'_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong \pi_1(K_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong G_{\mathcal{P}}$. By `smoothening the
  corners' we obtain the desired smooth manifold $M_{\mathcal{P}}$ smoothly embedded in
  ${\mathbb{R}}^5$ with $\pi_1(M_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong \pi_1(M'_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong G_{\mathcal{P}}$ ($M_{\mathcal{P}}$ is homotopy
  equivalent with $M'_{\mathcal{P}}$). But it also follows
  that $\pi_1(M_{\mathcal{P}}) \cong \pi_1(\partial M_{\mathcal{P}})$; see the proof of Lemma~3
  in~\cite{kirby20}. This establishes (i) and (ii).

  For (iii), if $G_{\mathcal{P}}$ is trivial, we first note that $H_2(\partial M)$ (and
  $H^2(\partial M)$) are free ${\mathbb{Z}}$-modules (there is no torsion). Indeed, this
  follows from the Poincaré duality and the universal coefficient theorem
  (using that $H_1(\partial M) = 0$). Thus it is sufficient to perform
  computations over ${\mathbb{Q}}$.
  Next we 
  note that the Euler characteristic of $K_{\mathcal{P}}$ equals $1 - n + m =
  1 + k$. (Computing the Euler characteristic is easy. This formula is, for
  example, mentioned below proof of Theorem~2.7 in Chapter I.
  of~\cite{hog-angeloni-metzler-sieradski93}.)  The Euler characteristic can be
  equivalently expressed as $\beta_0(K_{\mathcal{P}}) - \beta_1(K_{\mathcal{P}}) +
  \beta_2(K_{\mathcal{P}})$. If
  $G_{\mathcal{P}}$ is trivial, then $K_{\mathcal{P}}$ is simply connected and thus
  $\beta_1(K_{\mathcal{P}}) = 0$.
  Because $K_{\mathcal{P}}$ is connected, we also get $\beta_0(K_{\mathcal{P}}) = 1$. Thus we deduce
  that $\beta_2(K_{\mathcal{P}}) = k$. Consequently, $\beta_2(M_{\mathcal{P}}) = k$ as
  $M_{\mathcal{P}}$ and $K_{\mathcal{P}}$
  are homotopy equivalent. Finally, by `half lives, half dies';
  see~\cite{putman22} or \cite[Lemma 3.5]{hatcher07} (in the latter case, the
  proof is given only in dimension 3 but it extends to odd dimensions), we
  get $\beta_2(\partial M_{\mathcal{P}}) = 2k$.

nodes.statement: The intersection form of \#_k (CP^2 \# - CP^2) is well known---up to a choice of basis it is a form with diagonal matrix with k-times 1 and k-times -1; see. In particular, this form is odd. As a corollary of Wu's formula, explicitly stated in or, we get that the second Stiefel-Whitney class of the tangent bundle of N, that is w_2(T_N), is nontrivial. It follows that T_N is stably nontrivial; see Chapter~3, including Example~3.5, in. On the other hand, let us assume that N admits a smooth embedding into R^5. Then the tangent bundle of T_N is stably trivial as taking the direct sum with the normal bundle (from the embedding) yields a trivial bundle (coming from the trivial bundle on R^5 restricted to the embedding of N; see Section~1.1, `Direct Sums' in for an analogous example with spheres). A contradiction.
nodes.raw_latex:
The intersection form of $\#_k ({\mathbb{C}P}^2 \# - {\mathbb{C}P}^2)$ is well known---up to a choice
of basis it is a form with diagonal matrix with $k$-times $1$ and $k$-times
  $-1$; see~\cite{kirby89,scorpan05}. In particular, this form is odd. As a corollary of Wu's formula,
  explicitly stated in~\cite[Lemma~4.1, Chap. II]{kirby89} or~\cite[Sec.~4.3]{scorpan05}, we get that the second
  Stiefel-Whitney class of the tangent bundle of $N$, that is $w_2(T_N)$,
  is nontrivial. It follows that $T_N$ is
  stably nontrivial; see Chapter~3, including Example~3.5, in~\cite{hatcher17}. 
  
  On the other hand, let us assume that $N$ admits a smooth embedding into
  ${\mathbb{R}}^5$. Then the tangent bundle of $T_N$ is stably trivial as taking the
  direct sum with the normal bundle (from the embedding) yields a trivial
  bundle (coming from the trivial bundle on ${\mathbb{R}}^5$ restricted to the embedding
  of $N$; see Section~1.1, `Direct Sums' in~\cite{hatcher17} for an analogous
  example with spheres). A contradiction.

Then the tangent bundle of T_N is stably trivial as taking the direct sum with the normal bundle (from the embedding) yields a trivial bundle (coming from the trivial bundle on R^5 restricted to the embedding of N; see Section~1.1, `Direct Sums' in for an analogous example with spheres). A contradiction.

nodes.statement: Let P a presentation of deficiency k coming from the Adian-Rabin set in the statement. Let M_P be the manifold from Proposition~. We aim to show that partial M_P cong \#_k(S^2 times S^2) if and only if G_P (presented by P) is trivial. This will prove the result. If G_P is not trivial, then pi_1(partial M_P) is not trivial as well, by Proposition~(ii), which means that M notcong \#_k(S^2 times S^2). On the other hand, if G_P is trivial, then we also know that H_2(partial M) is a free product of 2k copies of Z by Proposition~(iii). As partial M bounds M, we deduce from Theorem~ that the signature of the intersection form Omega of partial M is zero. A fortiori, Omega must be indefinite. By characterization of indefinite forms, this leaves two options. The first one is that Omega is odd and p=q = k (using p and q as in characterization earlier). The second option is that Omega is even and r=0, s = k (again using r and s as in characterization earlier). The odd case can be realized by \#_k(CP^2 \# -CP^2) (see) while the even case can be realized by \#_k(S^2 times S^2) (see again). By Theorem~ we deduce that partial M is homeomorphic either to \#_k(CP^2 \# -CP^2) or \#_k(S^2 times S^2). However, the case \#_k(CP^2 \# -CP^2) can be excluded due to Proposition~(i) and Theorem~.

  the statement. Let $M_{\mathcal{P}}$ be the manifold from Proposition~\ref{p:M}. We aim to
  show that $\partial M_{\mathcal{P}} \cong \#_k(S^2 \times S^2)$ if and only if
  $G_{\mathcal{P}}$
  (presented by $\mathcal{P}$) is trivial. This will prove the result.

  If $G_{\mathcal{P}}$ is not trivial, then $\pi_1(\partial M_{\mathcal{P}})$ is not trivial as well, by
  Proposition~\ref{p:M}(ii), which means that $M \not\cong \#_k(S^2 \times S^2)$.

  On the other hand, if $G_{\mathcal{P}}$ is trivial, then we also 
  know that $H_2(\partial M)$ is a free product of $2k$ copies of
  ${\mathbb{Z}}$ by Proposition~\ref{p:M}(iii). 



  As $\partial M$ bounds $M$, we deduce from Theorem~\ref{t:rohlin} that the
  signature of the intersection form $\Omega$ of $\partial M$ is zero. A
  fortiori, $\Omega$ must be indefinite. By characterization of indefinite
  forms, this leaves two options. The first one is that $\Omega$ is odd and
  $p=q = k$ (using $p$ and $q$ as in characterization earlier). The second
  option is that $\Omega$ is even and $r=0$, $s = k$ (again using $r$ and $s$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem~\ref{t:ar_sequence}
nodes.statement: We order the words with the letters x_1, dots, x_n and their inverses into a sequence. For each such word we create a presentation P_w with the required deficiency such that P_w is trivial if and only if w is trivial. This way we get the required Adian-Rabin set. The generators of P_w are x_1, dots, x_n, alpha, beta, gamma. The relations are alpha^-1 beta alpha &= gamma^-1beta^-1gammabetagamma \\ alpha^-2beta^-1alphabetaalpha^2 &= gamma^-2beta^-1gammabetagamma^2 \\ alpha^-3walpha^3 &= gamma^-3betagamma^3 \\ alpha^-3+ir'_ibetaalpha^3+i &= gamma^-(3+i)betagamma^3+i and the relations r_1, dots, r_m of P. (Recall that r'_i are the additional relations from the statement of the theorem.) The change (when compared with Miller) in the third relation is only cosmetic. The changes in the last relations are important (and we have one relation for every r'_i). Each P_w has n+3 generators and m + m' + 3 relations, thereby it has the required deficiency. First, we show that if w is trivial, then P_w presents the trivial group. Indeed, if w is trivial, then we deduce that beta is trivial from the third relation. Consequently, we deduce that gamma is trivial from the first relation and that alpha is trivial from the second. Then we deduce that each r'_i is trivial from the last set of relations. This means that P_w is trivial due to our assumption. Now we assume that w is nontrivial and our aim is to show that P_w presents a nontrivial group. First we consider a free group G^RHS presented as langle beta, gamma| rangle with generators beta and gamma. Then beta together with the right hand sides of~-- form free generators of a subgroup of G^RHS. Indeed, an arbitrary product of powers of these elements or inverses is nontrivial in G^RHS as the middle portions of the word on the right hand side of~-- will persist.footnoteOf course, we consider only nontrivial products in reduced forms. That is, no g^i and g^-j appear next to each other if i, j in \1, 2, dots \ and g is either beta or a word on the right hand side of~--. Similarly, we consider a group G^LHS which is the free product P * langle alpha, beta rangle (identifying a group presentation with the group it presents). Then beta together with the left hand sides of~-- form free generators of a subgroup of G^LHS by the same argument as above, assuming that w is nontrivial. This means that P_w is a presentation of the free product G^LHS * G^RHS with amalgamation where the amalgamation is given by identifying the symbols beta and using the relations~--. This means that G^LHS and consequently P is a subgroup of P_w (again identifying groups and presentations). Therefore P_w is nontrivial.
nodes.raw_latex:
We order the words with the letters $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and their inverses into a
sequence. For each such word we create a presentation $\mathcal{P}_w$ with the required
deficiency such that $\mathcal{P}_w$ is trivial if and only if $w$ is trivial. This way
we get the required Adian-Rabin set. 

The generators of $\mathcal{P}_w$ are $x_1, \dots, x_n, \alpha, \beta, \gamma$. The
  relations are
\begin{align}
  \alpha^{-1} \beta \alpha &= \gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}\gamma\beta\gamma
  \label{eq:miller_1}\\
  \alpha^{-2}\beta^{-1}\alpha\beta\alpha^{2} &= 
  \gamma^{-2}\beta^{-1}\gamma\beta\gamma^{2} \\
  \alpha^{-3}w\alpha^{3} &= \gamma^{-3}\beta\gamma^3 \\
  \alpha^{-3+i}r'_i\beta\alpha^{3+i} &= \gamma^{-(3+i)}\beta\gamma^{3+i}
  \label{eq:miller_4}
\end{align}
  and the relations $r_1, \dots, r_m$ of $\mathcal{P}$. (Recall that $r'_i$ are
  the additional relations from the statement of the theorem.)
  
  The change (when compared with Miller) in the third relation is only cosmetic. The changes in the last
  relations are important (and we have one relation for every $r'_i$). Each
  $\mathcal{P}_w$ has $n+3$ generators and $m + m' + 3$ relations, thereby it has the
  required deficiency.  

First, we show that if $w$ is trivial, then $\mathcal{P}_w$ presents the trivial group.
Indeed, if $w$ is trivial, then we deduce that $\beta$ is trivial from the
  third relation. Consequently, we deduce that $\gamma$ is trivial from the
  first relation and that $\alpha$ is trivial from the second. Then we deduce
  that each $r'_i$ is trivial from the last set of relations. This means that
  $\mathcal{P}_w$ is trivial due to our assumption. 

Now we assume that $w$ is nontrivial and our aim is to show that $\mathcal{P}_w$
  presents a nontrivial group. First we consider a free group $G^{\mathrm{RHS}}$
  presented as $\langle \beta,
  \gamma| \rangle$ with generators $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Then
  $\beta$ together with the right hand sides
  of~\eqref{eq:miller_1}--\eqref{eq:miller_4} form free generators of a
  subgroup of $G^{\mathrm{RHS}}$. Indeed, an arbitrary product of powers of these elements or
  inverses is nontrivial in $G^{\mathrm{RHS}}$ as the middle portions of the word on
  the right hand side of~\eqref{eq:miller_1}--\eqref{eq:miller_4} will
  persist.\footnote{Of course, we consider only nontrivial products in reduced
  forms. That is, no $g^{i}$ and $g^{-j}$ appear next to each other if $i, j
  \in \{1, 2, \dots \}$ and $g$ is either $\beta$ or a word on the right hand
  side of~\eqref{eq:miller_1}--\eqref{eq:miller_4}.} Similarly, we consider a
  group $G^{\mathrm{LHS}}$ which is the free product $\mathcal{P} * \langle \alpha, \beta
  \rangle$ (identifying a group presentation with the group it presents). Then
  $\beta$ together with the left hand sides
  of~\eqref{eq:miller_1}--\eqref{eq:miller_4} form free generators of a
  subgroup of $G^{\mathrm{LHS}}$ by the same argument as above, assuming that $w$ is
  nontrivial. This means that $\mathcal{P}_w$ is a presentation of the free product
  $G^{\mathrm{LHS}} * G^{\mathrm{RHS}}$ with amalgamation where the amalgamation is given by
  identifying the symbols $\beta$ and using the
  relations~\eqref{eq:miller_1}--\eqref{eq:miller_4}. This means that
  $G^{\mathrm{LHS}}$ and consequently $\mathcal{P}$ is a subgroup of $\mathcal{P}_w$ (again identifying
  groups and presentations). Therefore $\mathcal{P}_w$ is nontrivial.

Let us assume that $P$ and $Q$ are equivalent in the Thue system. We want to
  show that $Q^{-1}tQk = kQ^{-1}tQ$ in $\mathcal{B}'$.
  It is sufficient to prove it in
  the case when $Q$ is obtained from $P$ by a single application of a rewriting
  rule in the Thue system and then to proceed by induction. Let us assume that
  $P = RF_iS$ and $Q = RE_iS$ for some words $R, S$ on the alphabet $\{s_1,
  \dots, s_N\}$ (without inverses) and $i \in [M]$. (The other case $P = RE_iS$
  and $Q = RF_iS$ is analogous.)

  Let $\makevec{d} := d^{g(i)\alpha^{|R|}}$, $\makevec{d}' := d^{g'(i)\alpha^{|R|}}$, $\makevec{e} :=
  e^{h(i)\alpha^{|S|}}$ and $\makevec{e}' := e^{h'(i)\alpha^{|S|}}$ where $|W|$ stands for
  the length of a word $W$. First we observe that the following equality holds
  in $\mathcal{B}'$:

  \begin{equation}
    \label{e:dPec}
    c\makevec{d}' Q \makevec{e}' = \makevec{d} P \makevec{e} c
  \end{equation}
Indeed
 \begin{align*}
   c\makevec{d}' Q \makevec{e}' &= c\makevec{d}' RE_iS \makevec{e}' \stackrel{(\ref{e:b1},\ref{e:b2})}{=}
   cRd^{g'(i)} E_i  e^{h'(i)} S  \stackrel{\eqref{e:b3}}{=} Rcd^{g'(i)} E_i
   e^{h'(i)} S
   \stackrel{\eqref{e:b4'}}{=} Rd^{g(i)} F_i e^{h(i)} cS \\
   &\stackrel{\eqref{e:b3}}{=} Rd^{g(i)} F_i e^{h(i)} Sc 
   \stackrel{(\ref{e:b1},\ref{e:b2})}{=} \makevec{d} RF_iS \makevec{e} c = \makevec{d} P \makevec{e} c. 
 \end{align*}
Now,

  \begin{tabular}{rcl}
    $Q^{-1}tQkQ^{-1}t^{-1}Qk^{-1}$
    &
    $\stackrel{(\ref{e:b5},\ref{e:b6},\ref{e:b8})}{=}$ &
    $\makevec{e}' \makevec{e}'^{-1} Q^{-1}   \makevec{d}'^{-1} c^{-1} t c
    \makevec{d}' Q\makevec{e}' k \makevec{e}'^{-1} Q^{-1} \makevec{d}'^{-1} c^{-1} t^{-1} c \makevec{d}' Q \makevec{e}' k^{-1}
    \makevec{e}'^{-1}$ \\
    &
    $\stackrel{\eqref{e:dPec}}{=}$ & $\makevec{e}' c^{-1} \makevec{e}^{-1} P^{-1} \makevec{d}^{-1} t \makevec{d} P
    \makevec{e} c k c^{-1} \makevec{e}^{-1} P^{-1} \makevec{d}^{-1} t^{-1} \makevec{d} P \makevec{e} c k^{-1}
    \makevec{e}'^{-1}$
    \\
    & $\stackrel{(\ref{e:b6},\ref{e:b7},\ref{e:b8})}{=}$ & $\makevec{e}' c^{-1} \makevec{e}^{-1}
    P^{-1} t P k P^{-1} t^{-1} P k^{-1} \makevec{e} c \makevec{e}'^{-1}$ \\
    & $\stackrel{\eqref{e:b9}}{=}$ & 1.
  \end{tabular}

nodes.statement: Let \[P = langle x_1, dots, x_p, c, y_1, dots, y_q| R, y_1 c = c y_1, dots, y_q c = c y_q rangle\] be a presentation where p, q are non-negative integers and R is an unspecified set of relations. Consider an encoding of letters of an alphabet Sigma = \x_1, dots, x_p, c, y_1, dots, y_q\ using words in an alphabet Sigma' = \x_1, dots, x_p, c, a, b\ given by mu(x_i) := x_i, mu(c) := c, mu(y_j) := w_j where each w_j is some aperiodic cyclically reduced word using only a and b (and their inverses). We also extend this encoding to the inverses (e.g. mu(y_j^-1) = w_j^-1) and to the words on letters of Sigma and their inverses (e.g. mu(x_iy_j^-1) = mu(x_i)mu(y_j^-1) = x_iw_j^-1). Assume that the set of (cyclically reduced) words W := \w_1, dots, w_q\ satisfies the metric small cancellation condition C'(1/6); in particular, it also satisfies C_sub(6). Assume also that if we add the relations \x_1, dots, x_p, y_1, dots, y_q\ to P, then we obtain a free group generated by c. (In other words, in every relator of R, the sum of the exponents of c is equal to 0.) Consider the presentation \[P' = langle x_1, dots, x_p, c, a, b| mu(R), ac = ca, bc = cbrangle,\] where mu(R) stands for \mu(r) colon r in R\. Then a word w is trivial in P if and only if mu(w) is trivial in P'.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{t:encoding}
  Let 
  \[\mathcal{P} = \langle x_1, \dots, x_p, c, y_1, \dots, y_q| R, y_1 c = c y_1, \dots,
  y_q c = c y_q \rangle\] 
  be a presentation where $p, q$ are non-negative integers and $R$ is an
  unspecified set of relations. 
 
  Consider an encoding of letters of an alphabet $\Sigma = \{x_1, \dots, x_p, c,
  y_1, \dots, y_q\}$ using words in an alphabet $\Sigma' = \{x_1, \dots, x_p, c,
	a, b\}$ given by $\mu(x_i) := x_i$, $\mu(c) := c$, $\mu(y_j) := w_j$ where each $w_j$  is some aperiodic cyclically reduced word using only $a$ and $b$ (and their inverses). We also extend this
  encoding to the inverses (e.g. $\mu(y_j^{-1}) = w_j^{-1}$) and to the words on
  letters of $\Sigma$ and their inverses (e.g. $\mu(x_iy_j^{-1}) =
  \mu(x_i)\mu(y_j^{-1}) = x_iw_j^{-1}$). Assume that the set of (cyclically
  reduced) words $W := \{w_1, \dots,
  w_q\}$ satisfies the metric small cancellation condition $C'(1/6)$; in
  particular, it also satisfies $C_{\mathrm{sub}}(6)$. Assume also

  that if we add
  the relations $\{x_1, \dots, x_p, y_1, \dots, y_q\}$ to $\mathcal{P}$, then we obtain a
  free group generated by $c$.


  (In other
  words, in every relator of $R$, the sum of the exponents of $c$ is equal to
  $0$.)

  Consider the presentation
  \[\mathcal{P}' = \langle x_1, \dots, x_p, c, a, b| \mu(R), ac = ca, bc = cb\rangle,\] 
  where $\mu(R)$ stands for $\{\mu(r) \colon r \in R\}$. Then a word $w$ is
  trivial in $\mathcal{P}$ if and only if $\mu(w)$ is trivial in $\mathcal{P}'$.

nodes.statement: Let us set P = B' where B' is the presentation from Theorem~. We consider B' specifically for Matiyasevich's Thue system and with g(1) = h(1) = h'(1) = 1, g'(1) = 2, g(2) = h(2) = g'(2) = h'(2) = 3, g(3) = h(3) = g'(3) = 4 and h'(3) = 5. We also consider an encoding mu given by formulas~--. It is trivial to check that these mu(s_1), mu(s_2), mu(k) and mu(t) are cyclically reduced and aperiodic. It is easy to check that the set of words \mu(s_1), mu(s_2), mu(k), mu(t)\ =\w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4\ satisfies the metric small cancellation condition C'(6). Indeed, let r in \w_1, w_2, w_3, w_4\^* where r is a cyclic shift of w_i. If r = ux where u is a piece, then u is of form a^j_1b^j_2 or b^j_1a^j_2 for integers j_1, j_2 with |j_1|, |j_2| leq 8 + 10i. Thus |u|leq 16 + 20i. On the other hand, |r| = |w_i| = 58 + 160i. Thus |u| < |r|/6 as required. We also easily verify the condition that if we add relations \s_1, s_2, d, e, k, t\ to B', then we get a free group generated by c. (If we rewrite the relations u_1 = u_2 containing c as u_1(u_2)^-1 = 1, then the sum of the exponents of c equals 0.) This means that we have verified the conditions of Theorem~. nodes.name: Proof of the `only if' part of Theorem~\ref{t:encoding}
nodes.statement: The `only if' part of the statement is easy: We first observe that the relations ac=ca and bc = cb in P' imply mu(y_j)c = cmu(y_j) for every j in [q] as mu(y_j) = w_j is a word using only a and b (and their inverses). Thus we can add the relations mu(y_j)c = cmu(y_j) to P' without changing the group it presents. Now we assume that w is trivial in P. Thus there is a van Kampen diagram witnessing that w is trivial in P. We subdivide each symbol y_j (or the inverse) in this diagram and replace it with mu(y_j) (or the inverse) while keeping the orientation. We obtain a van Kampen diagram witnessing that mu(w) is trivial in P' (some cells may use the relations mu(y_j)c = cmu(y_j) on their boundaries).

nodes.statement: Let G be a plane graph (i.e. a graph embedded in the plane) with n > 2 vertices, possibly with loops and multiple edges. Let us also assume that no two parallel edges (connecting the same two vertices) and no two parallel loops (attached to the same vertex) are isotopic by an isotopy fixing the endpoints and avoiding the other vertices. Let us also assume that the interior and the exterior of every loop contains a vertex. Then the number of edges of G is at most 3n -6.

nodes.name: Proof of the `if' part of Theorem~\ref{t:encoding}
nodes.statement: For the `if' part of the statement, we assume that mu(w) is trivial in P' and we want to deduce that w is trivial in P. First we need to check that certain words are nontrivial in P'. Let k be an integer. Then the words ac^k, bc^k are nontrivial in P'. If, in addition, k neq 0, then c^k is nontrivial in P'. First we show that c^k is nontrivial in P': For each letter s in Sigma different from c we add a relation mu(s) to the relations of P' and we also add relation a, b, obtaining a presentation P''. By comparing the relations of P and P', we obtain that P'' presents the same group as adding relations x_1, dots, x_p, y_1, dots, y_q to P. Therefore P'' is a free group generated by c. It means that c^k is nontrivial in P'' which implies that it is nontrivial in P' as well. Now, for contradiction, assume that ac^k is trivial in P'. (The proof is analogous for bc^k.) For each letter s in Sigma (including c) we add a relation mu(s) to the relations of P' obtaining a presentation P'''. As ac^k is trivial in P', we get that a is trivial in P'''. By checking the relations of P''', we see that we can remove the (trivial) letters x_1, dots, x_p and c and that every other relation is implied by relations mu(y_1), dots, mu(y_q), that is, the relations w_1, dots, w_q. This means that after removing the trivial letters P''' is equivalently presented as langle a, b| Wrangle. (Recall that W = \w_1, dots, w_q\.) By Lemma~, using C'(1/6), if a is trivial in langle a, b| Wrangle, then a subword of a is a subword of some u in W^* of length more than the half of the length of u. However, each word u in W^* has length at least two (actually more) which easily follows from the metric small cancellation condition C'(1/6) of W. (Actually C(6) is sufficient.) This contradicts that a is trivial in P'''. Let D' be a van Kampen diagram witnessing that mu(w) is a trivial word in P'. Given a 2-cell sigma in D' we say that is an R-cell, if its boundary label is of a form mu(r) for r in R^* (up to a cyclic permutation or taking an inverse). The only remaining cases are that the boundary label of sigma is either aca^-1c^-1 or bcb^-1c^-1 (up to a cyclic permutation or taking an inverse). In these cases, we say that sigma is a commutator cell. Given a 2-cell sigma in D', we say that sigma is regular if the closure of sigma is homeomorphic to a disk. Every commutator cell in D' is regular. Assume, for contradiction that there is a commutator cell sigma which is not regular. This means that the image of the closure of sigma is not simply connected and there is a (closed) disk D such that the boundary of D is formed by some proper subword of some cyclic permutation and possibly inverse of one of aca^-1c^-1 or bcb^-1c^-1. Up to a cyclic permutation and/or inverse, u is one of the words a, b, c, ac, ac^-1, bc, bc^-1 or some cyclically non-reduced word such as caa^-1. Each of these words is nontrivial due to Claim~. On the other hand, D' restricted to D (as D' is simply connected) proves that the aforementioned subword is trivial, which is the required contradiction. By an incidence pair we mean a pair (sigma, e) where item e is an edge labeled a, b, a^-1 or b^-1; and item sigma is an R-cell such that e appears on the boundary walk of sigma. We also allow sigma to be the outer face of the diagram (by the outer face we mean the complement of the diagram in R^2). If e appears on the boundary walk of sigma twice, then we have two distinct incidence pairs distinguished by whether sigma appears on the right-hand side or left-hand side. But we do not introduce an additional notation in this case. Now we define an auxiliary graph G embedded in R^2: The vertices of G are the midpoints of edges e labelled a, b, a^-1 or b^-1. Each edge of G is represented by a curve within some commutator cell sigma connecting the two midpoints of edges with labels a, b, a^-1 or b^-1. Note that G is embedded and its maximum degree is at most 2. Note also that the vertices of degree at most 1 correspond to (the edges of) incidence pairs whereas the vertices of degree 2 do not come from incidence pairs. Given two distinct incidence pairs (sigma, e) and (sigma', e'), we say that they are twins if the midpoints of e and e' are in the same component of G; see Figure~. Note that it may either happen that e = e' and the midpoint is an isolated vertex of G, or e neq e' and the midpoints of e and e' are of degree 1 in G. Note also that for each incidence pair there is a uniquely defined twin. We also remark that the edges of twins are always labelled with a same letter (if the orientations are suitably chosen). includegraphics[page=3]diagrams captionAn example of a part of a diagram showing the graph G and twins. The vertices of G are marked by small boxes, the edges of G are dashed. For example, the pairs (sigma_1, e_1) and (sigma_2,e_2) are twins where e_1 is the edge labelled a in sigma_1 and e_2 is the edge labelled a in sigma_2. Also the pairs (sigma_2, e_3) and (sigma_3, e_3) are twins where e_3 is the joint edge of sigma_2 and sigma_3. Now, given an incidence pair makevecp = (sigma, e), recall that the boundary label of sigma is of form mu(u) where u is a word over Sigma cup Sigma^-1 where Sigma^-1 stands for the set of inverses of letters in Sigma. In more detail, u might be either w (if sigma is the outer face), or some r in R otherwise. Given that mu(x_i) = x_i, mu(c) = c and mu(y_j) = w_j, we get that mu(u) is a concatenation of letters x_i, x^-1_i, c, c^-1 and words w_j and w_j^-1 for i in [p], j in [q]. We do not even claim that there is a unique way how to write the boundary word of sigma as such a concatenation (up to changing the orientation of sigma).footnoteWith some effort it actually follows from the assumptions of the theorem that this is unique for a fixed orientation of~sigma. But it does not help much in the proof of the theorem, thus we rather prefer not assume this. We only fix one such way for each sigma and use it consistently for all incidence pairs corresponding to sigma. Recall that e is labelled a, b, a^-1 or b^-1. This means that e is inside some word w_j or w_j^-1 in the concatenation above. (The decision between w_j or w_j^-1 depends only on the orientation of sigma.) Let us denote this word w(makevecp) (assuming that we specify the orientation of sigma). (Note that, in principle, w(makevecp) may also be the whole boundary label of sigma.footnoteHowever, this occurs only in a somewhat artificial case when some y_j (or its inverse) appears in R. In such case, y_j can be removed from the generators and relations without affecting the group presented by P.) Also the position of e within the word w(makevecp) is determined, let us denote by i(makevecp) this position. That is, the label of e is the i(makevecp)th letter of w(makevecp). Given twins makevecp = (sigma, e) and makevecp' = (sigma', e'), we say that makevecp and makevecp' are matched if the following holds: Once we pick opposite orientations of sigma and sigma', then w(makevecp) = w(makevecp') and i(makevecp) = i(makevecp'). In addition, we say that makevecp = (sigma, e) and makevecp' = (sigma', e') are fully matched if they are matched and if the following condition holds: For every j let e_j or e'_j be the jth edge of w(makevecp) = w(makevecp') when read along the boundary walk of sigma or sigma' (so that e = e_i(makevecp) and e' = e'_i(makevecp)).  edges $e_{i^- - 1}$ and $e'_{i^- - 1}$ and replace it with an edge $\bar
 e_{i^- - 1}$ (oriented according to the orientations of $\sigma$ and
 $\sigma'$ and keeping the label); see Figure~\ref{f:bigon}, right. This modification preserves the
 boundary labels of cells (those that haven't been removed). In addition,
 $(\sigma, \bar e_{i^- - 1})$ and $(\sigma', \bar e_{i^- - 1})$ is now pair of
 twins. This means that any pair of twins which was fully matched before the
 modification is still fully matched after the modification and we have
 extended the interval between $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ of matched pairs. After
 repeating this procedure now with the shared interval $[i_- -1, i^+]$ and
 using analogous procedure for $i_+ < h$, we will get all twins along the
 shared interval fully matched which is the required contradiction. (Of course, sometimes, we may fall into the
 case that $Q'$ is a path, which remains to be explained.)

 Now we assume that $Q'$ is a path. We take a regular neighborhood $N$ of $Q'$ and we modify $\mathcal{D}'$ inside

Let us think of $Q'$ as oriented in the plane so that the edges $e_{i_-}$ and
$e'_{i_-}$ enter $Q'$ from the right. We will take a copy of $Q'$ called $\bar
Q'$ connecting $v_1$ and $v'_1$ but shifting all other vertices of $\bar Q'$ a
little bit to the left (that is the vertices which originally belonged to $Q$.
For a vertex $z$ or $Q$ let $\bar z$ be the corresponding vertex on $\bar Q$.
Whenever some edge enters $z$ in $\mathcal{D}'$ from a left, we modify the diagram so that it now
enters $\bar z$ from the left (and we keep the edge outside $N$); see
Figure~\ref{f:matching_fully}, middle.

Now we orient and label $\bar Q'$ in the same way as $Q$. Then $Q'$ and $\bar
Q'$ bound a cell with a boundary label (word) of a form $\ell_{i_- -
1}\ell_{i_- - 1}^{-1}u\ell_{i_- -1}\ell_{i_- - 1}^{-1}u^{-1}$ where $u$ is a
word using only $c$ or $c^{-1}$. This cell can be easily filled with commutator
cells unless $u$ is trivial; see Figure~\ref{f:matching_fully}, right. If $u$
is trivial, we instead merge the vertices $v_1$ and $v'_1$ and the edges
connecting these vertices to $v_2 = v'_2$ as well as the edges
connecting them to $\bar v_2 = \bar v'_2$. This contracts the cell bounded by
$Q'$ and $\bar Q'$.  



It is easy to check that after these modifications we do not change boundary
labels of cells except possibly adding new commutator cells. In addition each
pair of fully matched twins remains fully matched (such twins were not touched
during the modification). After repeating this procedure now with the shared
interval $[i_- - 1, i_+]$ and using an analogous procedure if $i_+ < h$, we get

\begin{claim}
\label{c:fully_matched}
  Every pair of twins in $\mathcal{D}'$ is matched thereby fully matched.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
  For purpose of this proof we consider pairs $(\sigma, W)$ where $\sigma$ is
  some cell (or outer face) and
  $W$ is a subwalk  of the boundary walk of $\sigma$ which corresponds to some
  word $w_j = \mu(y_j)$. We say that $(\sigma, W)$ unmatched if for some edge
  $e$ of $W$, the incidence pair $(\sigma, e)$ is not matched with its twin.
  Because we already know that matched and fully matched is equivalent, this
  condition is equivalent with asking that for every edge $e$ of $W$, the
  incidence pair $(\sigma, e)$ is not matched with its twin. For contradiction,
  we assume that there is at least one unmatched pair $(\sigma, W)$.

  For each unmatched pair $\makevec{w} = (\sigma, W)$ we create (an image of) a disk $D_{\makevec{w}}$ in
  ${\mathbb{R}}^2$ in the following way. We push the boundary walk $W$ a little bit inside
  $\sigma$ while removing duplicated vertices. This way we obtain a path $\bar
  W$. (In a special case when $W$ corresponds to $w_j$ which is the
  whole boundary label of $\sigma$, $W$ starts and ends in a same
  vertex. Then we disconnect $W$ at the start/end-vertex when pushing. Thus
  $\bar W$ is still a path.)
  We thicken this path to a disk $D'_{\makevec{w}}$ inside $\sigma$ which is not yet
  $D_{\makevec{w}}$. We also require that distinct $\makevec{w}$ yield disjoint disks which can be achieved if we also
  shorten $\bar W$ a little bit before thickening to $D'_{\makevec{w}}$. See
  Figure~\ref{f:pushing_disks} for an example.
    
    \begin{figure}
      \begin{center}
	\includegraphics[page=5]{diagrams}
	\caption{Paths $\bar W$ and $\bar W'$ and disks $D'_{\makevec{w}}$ and
	$D'_{\makevec{w}'}$ for unmatched pairs $\makevec{w} = (\sigma, W)$ and $\makevec{w}' =
	(\sigma, W')$ where $W$ is a walk given by edges $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$
	and $W'$ is given by edges $e_4, \dots, e_8$.}
	\label{f:pushing_disks}
      \end{center}
    \end{figure}

  Now let us consider some incidence pair $\makevec{p} = (\sigma, e)$ such that $e \in W$.
  Let $\makevec{p}' = (\sigma', e')$ be a twin of $\makevec{p}$. Note that $\makevec{p}'$ corresponds to some unmatched
  pair $\makevec{w}' = (\sigma', W')$. Now we pull finger moves from disks $D'_{\makevec{w}}$
  and $D'_{\makevec{w}'}$ along the graph $G$ (the path connecting the midpoints of $e$
  and $e'$) so that the disks $D'_{\makevec{w}}$ and $D'_{\makevec{w}'}$ touch after this
  modification; see Figure~\ref{f:pulling_fingers} for an example. This we do
  for every pair of twins. This way we obtain the $D_{\makevec{w}}$. (Note that
  if $\makevec{w} = \makevec{w}'$, then pulling fingers causes that $D_{\makevec{w}}$ is not a closed
  disk anymore; however, the interior of $D_{\makevec{w}}$ is still an open disk.)


    \begin{figure}
      \begin{center}
	\includegraphics[page=6]{diagrams}
	\caption{Pulling fingers from the disks $D'_{\makevec{w}}$ along paths in graph
	$G$. The diagram corresponds to the diagram from Figure~\ref{f:twins}.}
	\label{f:pulling_fingers}
      \end{center}
    \end{figure}

  At this moment, we have a \emph{contact representation} of disks $D_{\makevec{w}}$
  (with possible self-identifications of the boundary). We
  consider the plane dual graph $H$ of this contact representation. The
  vertices of $H$ are points $v_{\makevec{w}}$ in $D_{\makevec{w}}$ and edges are curves inside the
  disks such that for each touching point there is exactly one edge passing
  through the touching point and connecting the vertices of the disks touching
  at this touching point. The edges do not cross.

We note that $H$ may contain loops and multiple edges.
  Now we argue that each loop in $H$ contains a vertex of $H$ both in its
  interior and its exterior. (By the interior, we mean the interior of the disk
  bounded by this loop and by the exterior we mean the plane minus this disk.)
  Indeed, for contradiction, let $\lambda$ be a loop in $H$ which does not contain a
  vertex of $H$ in its interior. In addition, we can assume that $\lambda$ is an
  innermost such loop. Let $v_{\makevec{w}}$ be the endpoint of the loop (i. e., the loop
  appears inside $D_{\makevec{w}}$). Locally, close  to $v_{\makevec{w}}$, the two arcs of
  $\lambda$ have to be consecutive because any other edge entering the interior
  of $\lambda$ would be either a loop inside $\lambda$ or a non-loop edge with other
  endpoint inside $\lambda$. Then the fact that the arcs of $\lambda$ are consecutive
  corresponds to the fact that the word $w_j$ contains (possibly after a cyclic
  shift) two consecutive letters $\ell\ell^{-1}$ where $w_j$ is the word read
  along the walk $W$, if $\makevec{w} = (\sigma, W)$. See Figure~\ref{f:no_empty_loop}
  for a nontrivial example when a cyclic shift is required. This contradicts the assumption
  that the words $w_j$ are cyclically reduced. An analogous argument, using the
  outermost loop, reveals that each loop contains a vertex in its exterior.

    \begin{figure}
      \begin{center}
	\includegraphics[page=18]{diagrams}
	\caption{A nontrivial example with an empty loop. In this example,
	$w_j$ would be of a form $\ell u \ell^{-1}$ when read in a clockwise direction
	along $\sigma$ where $u$ is another word. (The edges of the walk $W$ are thick.)}
	\label{f:no_empty_loop}
      \end{center}
    \end{figure}

Given two edges (possibly loops) of $H$, we say that they are \emph{equivalent}, if
they are isotopic via an isotopy fixing the endpoints and avoiding other
vertices of $H$. We build a graph $H'$ from $H$ by keeping the vertices and 
picking exactly one representative from each maximal collection of of
equivalent edges and loops. Now $H'$ satisfies the assumptions of
Lemma~\ref{l:mstw}, thus we conclude that $H'$ has at most $3n - 6$ edges
where $n$ is the number of vertices of $H$. 

Finally we aim to show that the degree of each vertex in $H'$ is at least $6$
which will yield the desired contradiction.



Consider a maximal collection $\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k$ of equivalent
edges (possibly loops). 
Assume that the endpoints of each of these edges
are $v_{\makevec{w}}$ and $v_{\makevec{w}'}$ with $\makevec{w} = (\sigma, W)$ and $\makevec{w}' = (\sigma',
W')$. (We have $\makevec{w} = \makevec{w}'$ if they are loops.) Then
$\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_k$ emanate from $v_{\makevec{w}}$ consecutively without loss of generality
in this order in the clockwise direction. (Here we already use that
each loop contains a vertex in the interior and in the exterior, otherwise an
empty loop could appear in between.) Subsequently, $\varepsilon_1, \dots,
\varepsilon_k$ emanate
from $v_{\makevec{w}'}$ consecutively in the counterclockwise direction. (We consider
the other ends of these edges, if they are loops.) According to the
construction of $H$, each $\varepsilon_i$ corresponds to a touching point of
$D_{\makevec{w}}$ and $D_{\makevec{w}'}$. The touching points appear consecutively exactly in the same order in
which $\varepsilon_i$ emanate from $v_{\makevec{w}}$ and $v_{\makevec{w}'}$ respectively.
The touching points of $D_{\makevec{w}}$ and $D_{\makevec{w}}$ are in a bijection with pairs of
  twins $\makevec{p} = (\sigma, e)$ and $\makevec{p}' = (\sigma',e')$ which are not matched.
  Furthermore $e$ belongs to some walk $W$ where $\makevec{w} = (\sigma, W)$ is an
  unmatched pair as well as $e'$ belongs to some walk $W'$ where $\makevec{w}' =
  (\sigma', W')$ is an unmatched pair. A collection of consecutive touching
  points along a boundary of $D_{\makevec{w}}$ as well as along the boundary $D_{\makevec{w}'}$
  corresponds to the fact that words $w(\makevec{p})$ and $w(\makevec{p}')$ possibly
  after a cyclic shift\footnote{A cyclic shift is necessary if the consecutive
  touching points are the first and the last touching point of $D_{\makevec{w}}$ or
  $D_{\makevec{w}}$ when the first and the last is considered in the order induced by
  $W$ or $W'$ respectively.} share a subpiece
  (formed by the labels of letters of the edges in pairs of twins corresponding
  to the touching points). Note that this is indeed a proper subpiece as either
  $w(\makevec{p}) \neq w(\makevec{p}')$ or $i(\makevec{p}) \neq i(\makevec{p}')$ because $\makevec{p}$ and $\makevec{p}'$ are
  not matched. (Here we also use our assumption that the words $w_j$ are
  aperiodic. It is used in the case that $w(\makevec{p}) = w(\makevec{p}')$ and $i(\makevec{p}) \neq
  i(\makevec{p}')$.) Due to the small cancellation property for subpieces $C_{\mathrm{sub}}(6)$, we get that
  $w(\makevec{p})$ meets this way at least six subpieces and thus
  there
  are at least six maximal collections of equivalent loops or multiple edges
  from each vertex of $H$. That is, the degree of each vertex in $H'$ is at
  least six.

Finally, given that the degree of each vertex in $H'$ is at least $6$, the
handshaking lemma (in graph theory) implies the number of edges of $H'$ is at least $3n$ which is a
contradiction with our earlier claim that the number of edges is at most
$3n-6$.
\end{proof}

Next we observe, by contradiction, that $G$ does not contain any cycle (that is $G$ is a disjoint
union of paths). Indeed, this is an immediate corollary of
Claim~\ref{c:1-grid} used on commutator cells $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k$ where
$\sigma_i$ is the commutator cell corresponding to $i$th edge of the cycle
(once we fix the first edge and an orientation). Then $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_k$
cannot close the cycle.


Now let $\kappa$ be a commutator cell. It corresponds to an edge in $G$ (passing
through $\kappa$) and consequently (because $G$ has no cycles) 
to a pair of twins $\makevec{p} = (\sigma, e)$ and $\makevec{p}' = (\sigma', e')$ such that the
path in $G$ connecting the midpoints of $e$ and $e'$ passes through $\kappa$. Let
$W(\makevec{p})$ be the walk on boundary of $\sigma$ corresponding to the word $w(\makevec{p})$
and $W(\makevec{p}')$ be the one on boundary of $\sigma'$ corresponding to $w(\makevec{p}')$.
Let $e_j$ be the $j$th edge of $W(\makevec{p})$ and $e'_j$ the $j$th edge of $W(\makevec{p}')$,
using the same conventions as when defining a fully matched pair. Due to
Claim~\ref{c:fully_matched}, we know that $w(\makevec{p}) = w(\makevec{p}')$ (in suitable
orientations) and setting $h$ to be the length of $w(\makevec{p})$ we also know that
$(\sigma,e_j)$ and $(\sigma', e'_j)$ are twins for every $j \in [h]$. Let $v_j$
be the $j$th vertex of $W(\makevec{p})$ and let
$v'_j$ be the $j$th vertex of $W(\makevec{p}')$ for $j \in [h+1]$. Finally, for $j \in
[h+1]$ let $Q^-_j = Q^-_j(\kappa)$ be the path from $v_j$ to $v'_j$
using only the edges labelled $c$ or $c^{-1}$ in commutator cells
along the path in $G$ connecting the midpoints of $e_j$ and
$e'_j$. By $Q^+_j = Q^+_j(\kappa)$ we denote the analogous path from $v_{j+1}$
to $v'_{j+1}$. (Here we use Claim~\ref{c:1-grid} to check that such paths
exist.)


\begin{claim}
\label{c:replace_commutators}
  The concatenation of walks $W(\makevec{p})$, $Q^+_{h}$, $W(\makevec{p}')$ (in opposite direction)
  and $Q^-_1$ (in opposite direction) forms a simple cycle. The diagram inside
  this cycle is isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w(\makevec{p}),k)$ for some $k > 0$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
  Let $j_1 \leq j_2$ be two elements of $[h]$ let $W_{j_1,j_2}(\makevec{p})$ (or
  $W_{j_1,j_2}(\makevec{p}')$) denote the subwalk of $W(\makevec{p})$
  (or $W(\makevec{p}')$) formed by the
  edges $e_j$ (or $e'_j$) for $j \in [j_1,j_2]$ respectively. Similarly, let
  $w_{j_1,j_2}(\makevec{p})$ be the word formed by the $j$th letters of $w(\makevec{p})$ for $j
  \in [j_1,j_2]$.
  

  Let $j_0 \in [h]$ be such that $e = e_{j_0}$. (That is, the path in $G$ 
  connecting the midpoints of $e$ and $e'$ intersects $\kappa$.) 
  

  We first show, by induction in $j_2$, that for every $j_2 \in [j_0,h]$ the concatenation of walks
  $W_{j_0,j_2}(\makevec{p})$,
  $Q^+_{j_2}$, $W_{j_0,j_2}(\makevec{p}')$ (in opposite direction) and $Q^-_{j_0}$ (in 
  opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this
  cycle is isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_0,j_2}(\makevec{p}),k)$ for some $k > 0$.

  From
  Claim~\ref{c:1-grid}, used on commutators along the path in $G$ connecting
  the midpoints of $e_{j_0}$ and $e'_{j_0}$ we get the first induction step if
  $j_2 = j_0$.
  
  For the second induction step, we assume that
  the concatenation of walks
  $W_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p})$,
  $Q^+_{j_2-1}$, $W_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p}')$ (in opposite direction) and $Q^-_{j_0}$ (in
  opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this
  cycle is isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p}),k)$ for some $k > 0$.
  Because $k > 0$, we in particular get that $v_{j_2} \neq v'_{j_2}$. This
  means that there is at least one commutator cell along the path connecting
  the midpoints of $e_{j_2}$ and $e'_{j_2}$. By Claim~\ref{c:1-grid}, used on
  commutators used along the aforementioned path, we get that 
  the concatenation of walks
  $W_{j_2,j_2}(\makevec{p})$,
  $Q^+_{j_2}$, $W_{j_2,j_2}(\makevec{p}')$ (in opposite direction) and $Q^-_{j_2}$ (in
  opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this
  cycle is isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_2,j_2}(\makevec{p}),k')$ for some $k' > 0$; see
  Figure~\ref{f:merge_grid} according to our current knowledge.

  \begin{figure}
    \begin{center}
      \includegraphics[page=16]{diagrams}
      \caption{Two concatenated walks during the induction with $k=3$ and
      $k'=4$.}
      \label{f:merge_grid}
    \end{center}
  \end{figure}

  Next we observe that $Q^+_{j_2-1}$ and $Q^-_{j_2}$ have to be identical. If
  this is not the case, then we get cycle with labels only $c$ or $c^{-1}$
  contradicting Claim~\ref{c:no_c-cycle}. However this already means that $k =
  k'$ and the diagrams isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p}),k)$ and
  $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_2,j_2}(\makevec{p}),k')$ in our notation merge to a diagram isomorphic with
  $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_0,j_2}(\makevec{p}),k)$ in our notation. (Note that the concatenation of
  walks $W_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p})$ and $W_{j_2,j_2}(\makevec{p})$ is just the walk
  $W_{j_0,j_2}(\makevec{p})$ and an analogous claim holds for walks $W'_{j_0,j_2-1}(\makevec{p})$
  etc.)

  If we use $j_2 = h$ in the claim we just proved: The concatenation of walks
  $W_{j_0,h}(\makevec{p})$,
  $Q^+_{h}$, $W_{j_0,h}(\makevec{p}')$ (in opposite direction) and $Q^-_{j_0}$ (in
  opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this
  cycle is isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(w_{j_0,h}(\makevec{p}),k)$ for some $k > 0$.

  Now, if we use an analogous induction in reverse direction (decreasing $j_0$
  down to $1$), we prove the required claim.
\end{proof}



Now we have acquired all tools to build a diagram $\mathcal{D}$ witnessing that $w$ is
a trivial word in $\mathcal{P}$. This will finish the proof of Theorem~\ref{t:encoding}.
In order to get $\mathcal{D}$ we will be relabelling some edges in $\mathcal{D}'$ as well as
merging some cells in $\mathcal{D}'$.

First we take care of commutator cells. Given a commutator cell $\kappa$, let
$W(\kappa)$ be the walk (cycle by Claim~\ref{c:replace_commutators}) obtained
by concatenation of $W(\makevec{p})$, $Q^+_h$,
$W(\makevec{p}')$ and $Q_1^{-}$ (last two in opposite directions) as in
Claim~\ref{c:replace_commutators}. In addition, let $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$ be the
subdiagram bounded by $W(\kappa)$. From Claim~\ref{c:replace_commutators} we
know that if $W(\kappa) \neq W(\kappa')$ for some other commutator cell
$\kappa'$, then $W(\kappa)$ and $W(\kappa')$ cannot be nested. Therefore, from
the construction of $W(\kappa)$ it follows that for $\kappa \neq \kappa'$
either $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa) = \mathcal{D}'(\kappa')$, or $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$ and $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa')$ are
disjoint possibly up to the boundary.

Now for any fixed $\kappa$ as above, we know that $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$ is isomorphic
to the grid diagram $\mathcal{G}(\makevec{w}(\makevec{p}), k)$ for some $k > 0$, using again the notation
from Claim~\ref{c:replace_commutators}. In addition, $\makevec{w}(\makevec{p}) = w_j$ for some
$j \in [q]$. We perform the following changes: We merge all edges of $W(\makevec{p})$
(considering $W(\makevec{p})$ oriented so that we read $\makevec{w}(\makevec{p})$ according to this
orientation without switching to inverses) into a single directed cell with the
same orientation. On this edge we put label $y_j$. Similarly, for $W(\makevec{p}')$ we
merge the edges into a single edge putting the label $y_j$ again. Then we
replace $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$ with the grid diagram $\mathcal{G}(y_j, k)$ so that we preserve
all orientations (possibly using reflections of the grid diagram); see
Figure~\ref{f:replace_commutators}. Note that these replacements are compatible
with the rest of the diagrams because $W(\makevec{p})$ and $W(\makevec{p}')$ are also walks on
boundaries of non-commutator cells. Therefore the inner vertices of $W(\makevec{p})$ or
$W(\makevec{p}')$ do not have neighbors outside $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$, thus replacing $W(\makevec{p})$
or $W(\makevec{p}')$ with a single edge is possible. (Of course, we also use that
$W(\makevec{p})$ and $W(\makevec{p}')$ are paths.)

\begin{figure}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[page=17]{diagrams}
    \caption{Replacement of commutator cells.}
    \label{f:replace_commutators}
  \end{center}
\end{figure}

We perform these replacements repeatedly as long as there is a commutator cell
$\kappa$ for which $\mathcal{D}'(\kappa)$ has not been replaced yet.

Now we consider an arbitrary $R$-cell $\sigma$ (or the outer face). If we
consider the boundary walk of $\sigma$, the word we originally read in $\mathcal{D}'$
was a concatenation of words $w_j$ for $j \in [q]$, or letters $x_i$ for $i \in
[p]$ or the letter $c$, or inverses of the aforementioned words and letters.
Some of $w_j$ might have been already replaced with $y_j$ due to treating
commutator cells. If there is however $w_j$ which haven't been replaced yet, we
consider the corresponding walk $W$ on the boundary of $\sigma$ representing
$w_j$. Due to the fact that every pair of twins is fully matched
(Claim~\ref{c:fully_matched}), this is also
a walk on boundary of a neighboring cell $\sigma'$ (it may happen that $\sigma
= \sigma'$). This means, that $W$ is actually a path. We orient this path in
the direction in which we read $w_j$ and we replace this path with an edge
labelled with same orientation labelled $y_j$.

We perform these replacements as long as there is a $\sigma$ and $w_j$
admitting such a replacement. After all these replacements we get the desired
diagram $\mathcal{D}$. In diagram $\mathcal{D}$ all occurrences of $w_j$ have been replaced with
$y_j$, other symbols have been either kept, or some symbols $c$ might have been
removed if they appeared inside some grid diagrams. However, in any case, for
the boundary word we have performed the inverse of the encoding $\ell \to
\mu(\ell)$ for all letters $\ell$ on the boundary, and similarly, for all cells
which we use in $\mathcal{D}$ we have also performed the inverse of the encoding. This
means that $\mathcal{D}$ witnesses that $w$ is a trivial word in $\mathcal{P}$.

For the second induction step, we assume that the concatenation of walks W_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp), Q^+_j_2-1, W_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp') (in opposite direction) and Q^-_j_0 (in opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this cycle is isomorphic with G(w_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp),k) for some k > 0. Because k > 0, we in particular get that v_j_2 neq v'_j_2. This means that there is at least one commutator cell along the path connecting the midpoints of e_j_2 and e'_j_2. By Claim~, used on commutators used along the aforementioned path, we get that the concatenation of walks W_j_2,j_2(makevecp), Q^+_j_2, W_j_2,j_2(makevecp') (in opposite direction) and Q^-_j_2 (in opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this cycle is isomorphic with G(w_j_2,j_2(makevecp),k') for some k' > 0; see Figure~ according to our current knowledge. includegraphics[page=16]diagrams captionTwo concatenated walks during the induction with k=3 and k'=4. Next we observe that Q^+_j_2-1 and Q^-_j_2 have to be identical. If this is not the case, then we get cycle with labels only c or c^-1 contradicting Claim~. However this already means that k = k' and the diagrams isomorphic with G(w_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp),k) and G(w_j_2,j_2(makevecp),k') in our notation merge to a diagram isomorphic with G(w_j_0,j_2(makevecp),k) in our notation. (Note that the concatenation of walks W_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp) and W_j_2,j_2(makevecp) is just the walk W_j_0,j_2(makevecp) and an analogous claim holds for walks W'_j_0,j_2-1(makevecp) etc.) If we use j_2 = h in the claim we just proved: The concatenation of walks W_j_0,h(makevecp), Q^+_h, W_j_0,h(makevecp') (in opposite direction) and Q^-_j_0 (in opposite direction) forms a simple cycle and the diagram inside this cycle is isomorphic with G(w_j_0,h(makevecp),k) for some k > 0. Now, if we use an analogous induction in reverse direction (decreasing j_0 down to 1), we prove the required claim. Now we have acquired all tools to build a diagram D witnessing that w is a trivial word in P. This will finish the proof of Theorem~. In order to get D we will be relabelling some edges in D' as well as merging some cells in D'. First we take care of commutator cells. Given a commutator cell kappa, let W(kappa) be the walk (cycle by Claim~) obtained by concatenation of W(makevecp), Q^+_h, W(makevecp') and Q_1^- (last two in opposite directions) as in Claim~. In addition, let D'(kappa) be the subdiagram bounded by W(kappa). From Claim~ we know that if W(kappa) neq W(kappa') for some other commutator cell kappa', then W(kappa) and W(kappa') cannot be nested. Therefore, from the construction of W(kappa) it follows that for kappa neq kappa' either D'(kappa) = D'(kappa'), or D'(kappa) and D'(kappa') are disjoint possibly up to the boundary. Now for any fixed kappa as above, we know that D'(kappa) is isomorphic to the grid diagram G(makevecw(makevecp), k) for some k > 0, using again the notation from Claim~. In addition, makevecw(makevecp) = w_j for some j in [q]. We perform the following changes: We merge all edges of W(makevecp) (considering W(makevecp) oriented so that we read makevecw(makevecp) according to this orientation without switching to inverses) into a single directed cell with the same orientation. On this edge we put label y_j. Similarly, for W(makevecp') we merge the edges into a single edge putting the label y_j again. Then we replace D'(kappa) with the grid diagram G(y_j, k) so that we preserve all orientations (possibly using reflections of the grid diagram); see Figure~. Note that these replacements are compatible with the rest of the diagrams because W(makevecp) and W(makevecp') are also walks on boundaries of non-commutator cells. Therefore the inner vertices of W(makevecp) or W(makevecp') do not have neighbors outside D'(kappa), thus replacing W(makevecp) or W(makevecp') with a single edge is possible. (Of course, we also use that W(makevecp) and W(makevecp') are paths.) includegraphics[page=17]diagrams captionReplacement of commutator cells. We perform these replacements repeatedly as long as there is a commutator cell kappa for which D'(kappa) has not been replaced yet. Now we consider an arbitrary R-cell sigma (or the outer face). If we consider the boundary walk of sigma, the word we originally read in D' was a concatenation of words w_j for j in [q], or letters x_i for i in [p] or the letter c, or inverses of the aforementioned words and letters. Some of w_j might have been already replaced with y_j due to treating commutator cells. If there is however w_j which haven't been replaced yet, we consider the corresponding walk W on the boundary of sigma representing w_j. Due to the fact that every pair of twins is fully matched (Claim~), this is also a walk on boundary of a neighboring cell sigma' (it may happen that sigma = sigma'). This means, that W is actually a path. We orient this path in the direction in which we read w_j and we replace this path with an edge labelled with same orientation labelled y_j. We perform these replacements as long as there is a sigma and w_j admitting such a replacement. After all these replacements we get the desired diagram D. In diagram D all occurrences of w_j have been replaced with y_j, other symbols have been either kept, or some symbols c might have been removed if they appeared inside some grid diagrams. However, in any case, for the boundary word we have performed the inverse of the encoding ell to mu(ell) for all letters ell on the boundary, and similarly, for all cells which we use in D we have also performed the inverse of the encoding. This means that D witnesses that w is a trivial word in P.

nodes.statement: First we show that c^k is nontrivial in P': For each letter s in Sigma different from c we add a relation mu(s) to the relations of P' and we also add relation a, b, obtaining a presentation P''. By comparing the relations of P and P', we obtain that P'' presents the same group as adding relations x_1, dots, x_p, y_1, dots, y_q to P. Therefore P'' is a free group generated by c. It means that c^k is nontrivial in P'' which implies that it is nontrivial in P' as well. Now, for contradiction, assume that ac^k is trivial in P'. (The proof is analogous for bc^k.) For each letter s in Sigma (including c) we add a relation mu(s) to the relations of P' obtaining a presentation P'''. As ac^k is trivial in P', we get that a is trivial in P'''. By checking the relations of P''', we see that we can remove the (trivial) letters x_1, dots, x_p and c and that every other relation is implied by relations mu(y_1), dots, mu(y_q), that is, the relations w_1, dots, w_q. This means that after removing the trivial letters P''' is equivalently presented as langle a, b| Wrangle. (Recall that W = \w_1, dots, w_q\.) By Lemma~, using C'(1/6), if a is trivial in langle a, b| Wrangle, then a subword of a is a subword of some u in W^* of length more than the half of the length of u. However, each word u in W^* has length at least two (actually more) which easily follows from the metric small cancellation condition C'(1/6) of W. (Actually C(6) is sufficient.) This contradicts that a is trivial in P'''.

nodes.statement: Assume, for contradiction that there is a commutator cell sigma which is not regular. This means that the image of the closure of sigma is not simply connected and there is a (closed) disk D such that the boundary of D is formed by some proper subword of some cyclic permutation and possibly inverse of one of aca^-1c^-1 or bcb^-1c^-1. Up to a cyclic permutation and/or inverse, u is one of the words a, b, c, ac, ac^-1, bc, bc^-1 or some cyclically non-reduced word such as caa^-1. Each of these words is nontrivial due to Claim~. On the other hand, D' restricted to D (as D' is simply connected) proves that the aforementioned subword is trivial, which is the required contradiction.

nodes.statement: For contradiction such a curve gamma exists. Let us pick an orientation of gamma and let u be the word that we read along gamma with respect to a given orientation. This word reduces to c^k where k is an integer. If k neq 0, we get a contradiction with Claim~ as gamma bounds a diagram with a boundary label reducing to c^k. It remains to consider the case k=0. In such case we adjust orientations of edges of gamma so that each label is c (and not c^-1). We have a same number of edges directed to the left as the number of edges directed to the right. We will obtain a new diagram D'' in the following way. We pick a pair of neighboring edges pointing out in opposite directions and we identify them by a contraction of the disk bounded by gamma (understood as a contraction of R^2; the result is again homeomorphic to R^2); see Figure~. We repeat this step until the disk bounded by gamma is contracted to a tree. includegraphics[page=9]diagrams captionA contraction of the disk bounded by gamma. We want to get a contradiction by showing that D' was not minimized with respect to the properties (P1) and (P2). We know that D'' has the same boundary label as D'. We also know that D'' has strictly less cells than D'. It remains to check that the number of twins in D'' which are matched but not fully matched is less than or equal to the number of those in D'. We observe that the graph G does not pass through gamma. Therefore the contractions we have performed did not affect matched and fully matched pairs outside gamma. On the other hand, we might have removed some matched pairs but not fully matched pairs inside gamma. Therefore D'' is better with respect to the properties (P1) and (P2) which is the required contradiction.

nodes.statement: The case k=1 is the contents of Claim~. We will spend the most effort with case k=2 which is essentially a straightforward case analysis ruling out all other options, using Claims~, and~. Then, for k geq 3, the claim will easily follow by induction. First we, therefore, assume k=2. Let P be a maximal path shared by boundaries of sigma_1 and sigma_2 containing an edge e labelled ell. Because we know that each commutator cell is regular (Claim~), we know that the edges preceding P and the edges following P along each of the boundaries are not shared. Let sigma be an open disk obtained by taking the union of sigma_1, sigma_2 and the interior of P. We can consider sigma as a cell in some other diagram obtained by removing the edges of P from D'. The boundary label of sigma with respect to some orientation is then some word that contains at most two pairs of edges labelled c and c^-1 and at most one pair of edges labelled ell and ell^-1. First we observe that the closure of sigma (which is the same as the closure of sigma_1 cup sigma_2) is a disk. If this is not the case, then the boundary walk of sigma decomposes in at least two cycles such that the words read along these cycles are some subwords u of the boundary label of sigma. Due to Claim~ we know that such a subword contains either ell or ell^-1. However, as we have at most one pair of edges labelled ell and ell^-1, and at least two cycles, we have exactly one occurrence of ell and ell^-1 together in each of these cycles. Due to simple connectedness u bounds some diagram, thus u is trivial in D'. But this contradicts Claim~. Now we know that the closure of sigma is a disk. We say that sigma_1 and sigma_2 is a reducing pair if we pick opposite orientations on sigma_1 and sigma_2 then we read the same word along the boundary of sigma_1 and sigma_2 when starting with e. We will show that sigma_1 and sigma_2 cannot be a reducing pair. Indeed, if sigma_1 and sigma_2 is a reducing pair, we orient the edges on the boundary of sigma according to the orientations of sigma_1 and sigma_2 and we perform a contraction of sigma identifying the labels which is possible since sigma_1 and sigma_2 is a reduction pair obtaining a diagram D''; see Figure~ for an example when P has length 1. includegraphics[page=10]diagrams captionA contraction of a reducing pair. The diagram D'' has the same boundary word as D' but it has less cells. The counts for property (P1) are the same in D'' and D' because by considering possible cases, the effect of contraction of a reducing pair on G is either a contraction of two edges (if P does not have two edges labelled ell or ell^-1) or removing a cycle on two edges from G (if P has two edges edges labelled ell or ell^-1). None of these changes affects matched or fully matched pairs of twins. Thus we get a contradiction that D' is a minimal graph satisfying (P1) and (P2). Thus, we get that sigma_1 and sigma_2 is not a reducing pair. By checking possible overlaps of the commutator cells, we get that the length of P is 1. Let us orient the edges on the boundary sigma_1 and sigma_2 so that we use only the labels ell and c (but not ell^-1 or c^-1). Then the fact that sigma_1 and sigma_2 is not a reducing pair translates so that the labelling of the edges on the boundary of sigma_1 and sigma_2 is as in Figure~ up to reverting all orientations of edges labelled ell and/or reverting all orientations of edges labelled c. In other words, the subdiagram formed by the closure of sigma is isomorphic to G(ell, 2). (Reverting orientations of these collections of edges corresponds to reflections. They may possibly swap the position of sigma_1 and sigma_2.) To finish the proof, we now assume that k geq 3 and that the claim is true for k-1. By induction, we know that the subdiagrams formed by closures of sigma_1 cup cdots cup sigma_k-1 and sigma_2 cup cdots cup sigma_k are isomorphic to G(ell, k-1). Therefore, the only way how not to arrive at a diagram isomorphic with G(ell,k) is if some vertex of sigma_1 not in sigma_2 is identified with some vertex sigma_k not in sigma_k-1. This however creates a cycle either with k labels c or k labels c and one label ell or ell^-1. This is a contradiction with Claim~ (taking the subdiagram bounded by the cycle).

  $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ then we read the same word along the boundary of
  $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ when starting with $e$. We will show that
  $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ cannot be a reducing pair.

  Indeed, if $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ is a reducing pair, we orient the edges
  on the boundary of $\sigma$ according to the orientations of $\sigma_1$ and
  $\sigma_2$ and we perform a contraction of $\sigma$ identifying the labels
  which is possible since $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ is a reduction pair
  obtaining a diagram $\mathcal{D}''$; see Figure~\ref{f:contract_reducing} for an
  example when $P$ has length 1.

    \begin{center}
      \includegraphics[page=10]{diagrams}
      \caption{A contraction of a reducing pair.}
      \label{f:contract_reducing}
    \end{center}
  \end{figure}

  The diagram $\mathcal{D}''$ has the same boundary word as $\mathcal{D}'$ but it has less
  cells. The counts for property (P1) are the same in $\mathcal{D}''$ and $\mathcal{D}'$
  because by considering possible cases, the effect of contraction of a
  reducing pair on $G$ is either a contraction of two edges (if $P$ does not
  have two edges labelled $\ell$ or $\ell^{-1}$) or removing a cycle on two
  edges from $G$ (if $P$ has two edges edges labelled $\ell$ or $\ell^{-1}$).
  None of these changes affects matched or fully matched pairs of twins. Thus
  we get a contradiction that $\mathcal{D}'$ is a minimal graph satisfying (P1) and
  (P2).  

  Thus, we get that $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ is not a reducing pair. By
  checking possible overlaps of the commutator cells, we get that the length of
  $P$ is 1. Let us orient the edges on the boundary $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$
  so that we use only the labels $\ell$ and $c$ (but not $\ell^{-1}$ or
  $c^{-1}$). Then the fact that $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ is not a reducing
  pair translates so that the labelling of the edges on the boundary of
  $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ is as in Figure~\ref{f:two_commutators} up to
  reverting all orientations of edges labelled $\ell$ and/or reverting all
  orientations of edges labelled $c$. In other words, the subdiagram formed by
  the closure of $\sigma$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal{G}(\ell, 2)$. (Reverting
  orientations of these collections of edges corresponds to reflections. They
  may possibly swap the position of $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.)

  To finish the proof, we now assume that $k \geq 3$ and that the claim is true
  for $k-1$. By induction, we know that the subdiagrams formed by closures of
  $\sigma_1 \cup \cdots \cup \sigma_{k-1}$ and $\sigma_2 \cup \cdots \cup
  \sigma_k$ are isomorphic to $\mathcal{G}(\ell, k-1)$. Therefore, the only way how not
  to arrive at a diagram isomorphic with $\mathcal{G}(\ell,k)$ is if some vertex of
  $\sigma_1$ not in $\sigma_2$ is identified with some vertex $\sigma_k$ not in
  $\sigma_{k-1}$. This however creates a cycle either with $k$ labels $c$ or
  $k$ labels $c$ and one label $\ell$ or $\ell^{-1}$. This is a contradiction
  with Claim~\ref{c:nontrivial} (taking the subdiagram bounded by the cycle).

nodes.statement: Assuming that D' contains a pair of twins which is matched but not fully matched, we will modify the diagram so that we keep the boundary word and we decrease the number of matched pairs which are not fully matched. This will contradict property (P1). Let makevecp = (sigma, e) and makevecp' = (sigma', e') be a matched pair of twins in D' which is not fully matched. Let us fix opposite orientations on sigma and sigma'. Let us write w(makevecp) = w(makevecp') as ell_1 ell_2 cdots ell_h where each ell_j is a, b, a^-1 or b^-1. Let i := i(makevecp) = i(makevecp'). Then we get that e as well as e' is labelled with ell_i. Let e_j or e'_j be the jth edge of w(makevecp) = w(makevecp') when read along the boundary walk of sigma or sigma'. We get that e_j as well as e'_j is labelled with ell_j. Let [i_-, i_+] be a maximum interval containing i such that for every j in [i_-, i_+] we get that (sigma, e_j) and (sigma', e'_j) are twins. This interval may contain only one element i but we know that it is not [h] because makevecp and makevecp' are not fully matched. We will assume that i_- > 2 and we will modify the diagram so that we extend the maximum shared interval to [i_- - 1, i_+] while keeping all other fully matched pairs and keeping the number of incidence pairs. Analogous procedure can be also used if i_+ < h. Therefore, after a finite number of steps, we extend the shared interval to [h] = [1,h] thereby obtaining new fully matched pairs. Let us denote some of the vertices of our diagram v_1, dots, v_h+1 so that the walk v_1, e_1, v_2, e_2, dots, e_h, v_h+1 is the walk along which we read the word w(makevecp) in sigma. (See Figure~, left.) Analogously, we denote v'_1, dots v'_h+1 along sigma'. Let P be the path in graph G connecting the midpoints of the edges e_i_- and e'_i_-. This path may possibly consist of a single vertex. Then, using Claim~ on commutator cells along P, there is a unique path Q (possibly trivial) from v_i_- to v'_i_- in D' such that each edge of Q is parallel with some edge of P within some commutator cell. Following the direction form v_i_- to v'_i_-, this path Q uses only the edges of commutator cells all labelled c or all labelled c^-1. By Q' we denote the walk obtained from Q by prepending the vertex v_i_- -1 and the edge e_i_- -1 and by appending the edge e'_i_- -1 and the vertex v'_i_- -1. The labels of edges of Q' are c, c^-1, ell_i_- -1 or ell_i_- -1^-1. includegraphics[page=4]diagrams captionLeft: An example of a diagram D' with a pair of twins which is matched but not fully matched. Here [i_-, i_+] = [2,3], Q' is denoted by thick edges and N is in gray. Middle: First modifications of D'; N is drawn slightly thicker for an easier visualisation. Right: The second modification, adding the commutator cells, up to a homeomorphism for easier visualisation. We will distinguish whether Q' is a path or not. We start with the case that Q' is not a path. Because Q is a path while Q' is not a path, this means that either one of the vertices v_i^- - 1 or v'_i^- - 1 is identified with a vertex of Q or v_i^- - 1 = v'_i^- - 1. Therefore v_i^- - 1 = v'_i^- - 1 and they are distinct from any vertex of Q. In addition Q has to consist of a single vertex, otherwise we get a contradiction with Claim~ again (all edges along Q have a same label c or c^-1 when Q is oriented from v_i^- to v'_i^-). That is, v_i^- = v'_i^-. However, e_i^- -1 neq e'_i^- -1 because we assume that (sigma, e_i^- -1) and (sigma', e'_i^- -1) are not twins; see Figure~, left. This modification preserves the boundary labels of cells (those that haven't been removed). In addition, (sigma, bar e_i^- - 1) and (sigma', bar e_i^- - 1) is now pair of twins. This means that any pair of twins which was fully matched before the modification is still fully matched after the modification and we have extended the interval between sigma and sigma' of matched pairs. After repeating this procedure now with the shared interval [i_- -1, i^+] and using analogous procedure for i_+ < h, we will get all twins along the shared interval fully matched which is the required contradiction. (Of course, sometimes, we may fall into the case that Q' is a path, which remains to be explained.) includegraphics[page=12]diagrams captionResolving the case when Q' is not a path. (In the drawing we assume that i^- = 2.) Now we assume that Q' is a path. We take a regular neighborhood N of Q' and we modify D' inside this regular neighborhood. Because Q' is a path we know that N is a disk. Let us think of Q' as oriented in the plane so that the edges e_i_- and e'_i_- enter Q' from the right. We will take a copy of Q' called bar Q' connecting v_1 and v'_1 but shifting all other vertices of bar Q' a little bit to the left (that is the vertices which originally belonged to Q. For a vertex z or Q let bar z be the corresponding vertex on bar Q. Whenever some edge enters z in D' from a left, we modify the diagram so that it now enters bar z from the left (and we keep the edge outside N); see Figure~, middle. Now we orient and label bar Q' in the same way as Q. Then Q' and bar Q' bound a cell with a boundary label (word) of a form ell_i_- - 1ell_i_- - 1^-1uell_i_- -1ell_i_- - 1^-1u^-1 where u is a word using only c or c^-1. This cell can be easily filled with commutator cells unless u is trivial; see Figure~, right. If u is trivial, we instead merge the vertices v_1 and v'_1 and the edges connecting these vertices to v_2 = v'_2 as well as the edges connecting them to bar v_2 = bar v'_2. This contracts the cell bounded by Q' and bar Q'. It is easy to check that after these modifications we do not change boundary labels of cells except possibly adding new commutator cells. In addition each pair of fully matched twins remains fully matched (such twins were not touched during the modification). After repeating this procedure now with the shared interval [i_- - 1, i_+] and using an analogous procedure if i_+ < h, we get all twins along the shared interval are fully matched. We have increased the number of fully matched pairs as required which proves the claim.
